newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala to begin regulating securities market.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala to begin regulating securities market.

text.p: A new government office to regulate Guatemala's small securities market should boost investment activity, government officials and managers of securities exchanges said on Thursday.

"It is very good for the development of the capital market to have a registry. This helps to lend security," said Rolando San Roman, general manager of the Bolsa de Valores Nacional, S.A., which has about 65 percent of the Guatemalan market.
San Roman was watching as President Alvaro Arzu cut the ribbon on the offices of the new Stock Market Registry Thursday.

"The exchanges will enter a new era because if we do an efficient job, market operations can increase and there could be more stocks in which the public has confidence," Joaquin Alvarado, who will head the new registry office, told Reuters.
Alvarado said there was absolutely no regulation of the market until last year when congress passed a securities law which established the new registry.
The Bolsa de Valores Nacional has been in existence since 1986. Two smaller exchanges, the Bolsa Agricola Nacional and Bolsa de Valores Global, went into business later.

The Bolsa de Valores Nacional deals 99 percent in debt. Some 150 companies, including banks, offer commercial paper with maturities of up to five years. The exchange also lists stocks of seven companies with a total market capitalization of about $140 million.
The other two exchanges also trade debt but Alvarado said with the new registry overseeing the market, more companies will be interested in selling stock.
"The registry exists so that investors will have true and current information from issuing companies," Alvarado said.

Whereas emission of stock outside an exchange is illegal in most countries Guatemala will try to prevent black market and pyramid schemes by requiring off-the-exchange stocks to register, Alvarado said.
The registry can also sanction insider trading with fines between $8,300 and $83,000, and refer cases of insider trading to the state prosecutor to initiate criminal proceedings, he said.
